openers.restoring-land-and-forests: Since 2021 the United Nations has run a campaign to repair the world's degraded ecosystems. This chapter asks how that repair works and who pays for it. Some projects bring back lost forests, some plant trees where none recently grew, and some step back so natural processes can return. Payments, credits and tax breaks reward replanting, while Africa's {{ref:nature-nbs-126}}, adopted in 2007, shows both the ambition and the difficulty. Running through it all is a debate over whether repairing nature can stand in for quickly cutting fossil fuel emissions.

nature-nbs-107.title: Reforestation: growing back the forests that were lost
nature-nbs-107.text: Up to 90% of newly planted seedlings often fail. That sobering figure hangs over reforestation, the work of restoring forests and woodlands that once stood on a site but were destroyed or damaged. The earlier loss may have come from deforestation, clearcutting or wildfire. Reforestation differs from {{ref:nature-nbs-102}}, which makes new forest on land that was not forest before. Programs have three main purposes: growing wood to harvest, slowing climate change, and restoring ecosystems and habitat. On the climate side, growing forests and cutting deforestation store more carbon in four ways. They enlarge forests, make them denser in carbon, replace fossil fuels with forest products, and avoid the emissions that forest loss releases. Yet new trees take decades to match mature tropical forests. That is why reducing deforestation usually helps the climate more than replanting does. The choice of tree matters as well. Some species, such as Eucalyptus globulus, draw so much water from the soil that other plants cannot grow. And large programs, such as China's Three-North program begun in 1978, blur the line between restoring old forest and creating new.

nature-nbs-102.title: Afforestation: planting forests where none recently stood
nature-nbs-102.text: Planting a forest on bare land sounds like an unmixed good. Researchers are not so sure. Afforestation is creating a forest or stand of trees on land that has had no recent tree cover. It differs from reforestation, which turns land that once held forest back into forest. There are three types: natural regeneration, growing trees among crops as in {{ref:nature-nbs-247}}, and plantations. The case for it is strong. Trees store carbon, so new ones can help slow climate change, the link traced in {{ref:nature-nbs-103}}. New trees can also raise local rainfall, block strong winds, and reduce soil erosion, floods and landslides. Projects create jobs, especially in rural areas, and supply wood products. The work starts with the site. Planners study its climate, soil, vegetation and human use, and these decide which species to plant and how. Australia, Canada, China, India, Israel, the United States and Europe all run programs, some also to reduce desertification. Still, researchers debate whether afforestation always helps, especially where land was never forest. Planting trees is not the only way to capture carbon.

nature-nbs-112.title: Ecological restoration: repairing ecosystems already damaged
nature-nbs-112.text: Hundreds of thousands of restoration projects now run worldwide, and their number has grown exponentially. Ecological restoration is helping an ecosystem recover after it has been degraded, damaged, destroyed or transformed. That sets it apart from conservation, which tries to prevent damage in the first place. Restoration repairs what is already harmed. The methods are hands-on: controlling erosion, replanting forests, removing weeds and non-native species, reintroducing native species and building wildlife corridors. The reasons vary just as much. Projects aim to restore natural capital such as clean water, help endangered species, adapt to climate change and store carbon. Done well, restoration can help reverse biodiversity loss, keep ecosystem services flowing and support local economies. The field has two halves. Restoration ecology is the scientific study; ecological restoration is the practical work. The record is mixed. Restorations often miss their goals, and their high costs can be seen as a drawback. Public support fades if the costs seem to outweigh the benefits. Even so, the United Nations named 2021–2030 a decade devoted to this work, the {{ref:nature-nbs-137}}.

nature-nbs-131.title: Rewilding: stepping back so nature can run itself
nature-nbs-131.text: In a Guyana forest, going from 5 to 35 mammal species raised the carbon in trees and soil four to five times. Results like that fuel interest in rewilding, a kind of ecological restoration that aims to raise biodiversity and restore natural processes while reducing human influence. Its key move is to replace human management with natural processes. Unlike other restoration, it accepts new mixes of species and interactions, the kind described in {{ref:nature-nbs-150}}. It often brings back large mammals to rebuild food webs, so that ecosystems regulate themselves. A group called Earth First coined the term in 1990. In 1998 Michael Soulé and Reed Noss gave it a scientific basis built on 'cores, corridors and carnivores': large protected areas, links between them, and large predators. Supporters promote it as a natural climate solution through carbon storage, flood management and lower wildfire risk. It is also controversial. Critics question its evidence and its effect on farming and livelihoods.

nature-nbs-109.title: Paying people to plant forests or leave them standing
nature-nbs-109.text: A standing forest earns nothing for the person who could have cut it down. Financial incentives try to change that sum. They are payments, credits and tax breaks that reward landowners or countries for replanting forests or for not cutting them down. One proposal, 'compensated reduction', would pay developing countries that cut emissions from deforestation over an agreed period. Joining would be voluntary. But a country that signs up must cut emissions, and a missed target rolls into its next period. An emerging source of money is the sale of carbon sequestration credits to companies and people offsetting their footprint. Such credits let farmers and private landowners earn money from replanting while gaining healthier soil. Governments also offer tax breaks to encourage companies to support reforestation.

nature-nbs-108.title: Plantation forests: trees in rows, grown for wood
nature-nbs-108.text: Over 90% of the world's forests regrow naturally rather than by planting. Plantation forests are the opposite extreme. They are intensively managed stands of one or two tree species of the same age, planted in regular rows mainly to produce wood. They cover about 131 million ha: 3% of the world's forest area and 45% of all planted forest. The other 55 percent of planted forest is not intensively managed and may come to resemble natural forest, serving restoration and soil and water protection. Planted forests are growing. Between 1990 and 2015 they rose from 4.1% to 7.0% of total forest area. Of their area worldwide, 18% holds exotic species and the rest native ones. Plantations are often single-species stands, the pattern explored in {{ref:nature-nbs-082}}, and that brings drawbacks such as biodiversity loss.

nature-nbs-137.title: The UN Decade on Ecosystem Restoration, 2021 to 2030
nature-nbs-137.text: About half the world's GDP depends directly on nature. Yet people use up natural resources about 1.6 times faster than nature restores them. The UN Decade on Ecosystem Restoration is a United Nations campaign, running from 2021 to 2030, to promote the repair of degraded ecosystems worldwide. El Salvador proposed it. The UN General Assembly adopted it on 1 March 2019, and it began on World Environment Day, 5 June 2021. UNEP and the Food and Agriculture Organization co-lead it. The UN defines restoration here as halting and reversing degradation so that ecosystem services improve and biodiversity recovers. The goals are to fight climate change, protect biodiversity, and improve food security and water supply. Nations were asked to deliver existing restoration pledges of over 1 billion hectares, an area bigger than China. Recommended approaches include {{ref:nature-nbs-258}}, ecological restoration and rewilding.

nature-nbs-117.title: Can restoring nature replace cutting emissions?
nature-nbs-117.text: Planting trees and healing land feels like progress, but its climate benefits are described as dwarfed by ongoing fossil fuel emissions. That gap sits at the center of a debate over relying on nature restoration to fight climate change instead of quickly cutting fossil fuel emissions. One study concluded that restoring land matters but cannot make up for delays in cutting fossil fuel emissions. It is too slow to lower peak temperatures in the coming decades. The kind of action matters too. Avoiding deforestation is better than clearing and replanting, because clearing causes lasting biodiversity loss and soil damage. The money side is contested as well. Offsetting carbon through forestry, where polluters pay for trees to balance their emissions, is controversial. Critics sometimes call it carbon colonialism. Sources still dispute how much weight restoration should carry against cutting fossil fuel use. On one point they agree: restoration cannot simply replace the cuts.

nature-nbs-126.title: Africa's Great Green Wall: a belt of trees across the Sahel
nature-nbs-126.text: The plan was a wall of trees 15 km wide and 7,775 km long. The Great Green Wall is an African Union project, adopted in 2007, first meant to stop desertification in the Sahel by planting a belt of trees from Djibouti to Senegal. It has since grown into a mosaic of green, productive landscapes using water harvesting and local land-use methods. By 2030 it aims to restore 100 million hectares of degraded land, capture 250 million tonnes of carbon dioxide and create 10 million jobs. Progress has been slow. A 2020 UNCCD report found only 4% of the planned area covered. In January 2021 partners pledged USD 14.3 billion, but by March 2023 only $2.5 billion had been paid out. As of 2024, about 30 million hectares had been restored, 30% of the target. Critics question its progress, funding and colonial framing, and some call for scrapping it. In 2023 it was said to face collapse from terrorism, weak leadership and too little funding.

nature-nbs-155.title: Species reintroduction: returning animals and plants to the wild
nature-nbs-155.text: Bringing wolves back can curb too many deer. Species reintroduction is deliberately releasing a species into the wild, from captivity or from other places, where it can survive. The aim is a healthy, genetically varied, self-sustaining population where the species had died out, or a boost to one that remains. Candidates are usually threatened or endangered, but pest control is another reason. Individuals come from wild populations, called in situ, or from zoos and botanic gardens, called ex situ. Wild sourcing is preferred where possible, and the source should resemble the release site. Captive-bred animals can become tamer and less stress-tolerant, and lose local adaptations. Small released populations risk inbreeding, which erodes genetic diversity. There is no agreed definition of success, but it should mean viable populations that sustain themselves long term.

nature-nbs-150.title: Novel ecosystems: nature in mixes never seen before
nature-nbs-150.text: A quarry colonized by weedy species. A coral reef taken over by algae. Both are novel ecosystems: places that human activity, land use and climate change have pushed into a mix of species and conditions never seen before. The term was first used in 2006. Three features define them. They have changed past a threshold, people caused the change, and afterward they sustain themselves without ongoing human management. They could become the norm. Without rapid climate action, they could cover more than 50% of Earth's land by 2100 and 80% by 2300. Some scientists argue that even when an ecosystem cannot return to its original state, a novel ecosystem's functions are still valuable. Researchers disagree on how to define novelty, and some argue against any sharp definition at all.

nature-nbs-145.title: Land restoration: returning land to a chosen state
nature-nbs-145.text: Restoring land starts with a choice: restore it to what? Land restoration, which may include rewilding, is returning land to a different or earlier state for a chosen purpose. The purposes vary. A project might make land safe, stabilize its ecological communities, clean up pollution, create a {{ref:nature-nbs-150}} or return land to a historical condition. Restoration answers damage caused mostly by people, such as pollution, deforestation, salination and species endangerment. It differs from land reclamation, which alters or destroys ecosystems to make way for farming or building. The payoff can be economic, because restored land can supply more valuable ecosystem services. Projects begin by surveying existing conditions. They then choose a reference ecosystem, a real or described system to measure success against. Increasingly, the mainstream approach uses traditional ecological knowledge alongside Western science.

nature-nbs-143.title: Land rehabilitation: making damaged ground useful again
nature-nbs-143.text: Mining, farming and forestry are among the activities that degrade land. Land rehabilitation is returning damaged land, for example after industry or natural disasters, to some degree of its former state. The goal is partial recovery, not a perfect copy. Words differ by place. In parts of the United States, 'reclamation' means returning disturbed land to an improved state. Mines show the methods most clearly. Rehabilitation reshapes waste dumps so they resist erosion, covers them with topsoil and plants vegetation to hold the material in place. Ore that contains sulfide minerals poses a special risk. Rain and air can turn it into sulfuric acid, so it is covered with clay to keep them out. Even closed mines can be put back to work. They can be reused for heat, water or methane recovery, which also keeps the methane out of the air.

nature-nbs-110.title: When new forests compete with farms and homes
nature-nbs-110.text: Government pledges to replant forests add up to 1.2bn hectares by 2060, a tenth of the world's land area, a total seen as unrealistic. Land is the catch. Reforestation can take land and water needed for food, grazing and housing, and may push out the people who use that land. Almost 300 million people live on land in the Global South identified as a tropical forest restoration opportunity. A WRI and IUCN map of 2 billion hectares for forest restoration is criticized for including 900 million hectares of grassland. Programs focused on carbon rather than nearby communities' needs have drawn criticism. Growing coffee under trees shows one way to blend forests with other uses.

nature-nbs-111.title: Will the carbon stored in new forests stay put?
nature-nbs-111.text: A forest that burns gives its carbon back. Permanence is the risk that carbon stored by reforestation returns to the air, through fire, insect outbreaks or harvesting. Harvesting and using wood from reforested land limits how long its carbon stays stored. Nearly half of the pledges under the {{ref:nature-nbs-139}} were found to be areas set aside for commercial wood use. Emissions from damage to tropical rainforests may also be underestimated by a factor of six. To manage such reversals, many carbon standards hold buffer reserves of credits and keep monitoring.

nature-nbs-105.title: Why dark new forests can warm the planet
nature-nbs-105.text: Trees are darker than snow. New forest canopy can darken Earth's surface, lowering the share of sunlight it reflects, a measure explained in {{ref:nature-nbs-090}}. The surface then absorbs more heat and may warm the planet. The effect matters most in snowy regions, where white snow reflects far more sunlight than dark forest. That extra heat could cancel part of the carbon benefit of afforestation. A 2023 study using 176 flux stations found a clear trade-off: more carbon uptake comes with a darker, less reflective surface. Tropical reforestation is different, because it helps form clouds that reflect sunlight and lower temperatures.

nature-nbs-104.title: Should trees be planted on grasslands and savannas?
nature-nbs-104.text: Not every treeless place is a damaged forest. Some tree-planting campaigns put forests where they would not grow naturally, such as grasslands and savannas, and critics object. They say treeless ecosystems are not necessarily degraded and can already store carbon. Savannas and tundra keep theirs underground. Grasslands and savannas need their own management, since they are not meant to be forests. Carbon forecasts for such programs often leave out soil carbon losses and the slowing of tree growth over time. Whether planting trees on naturally open land helps or harms remains debated.

nature-nbs-106.title: Single-species plantations: tree cover without the wildlife
nature-nbs-106.text: A dense stand of conifers lets little light reach the forest floor. Critics of planting forests of a single tree species point to such stands: tree cover rises, but the varied habitat wildlife needs is missing. These plantations are often grown for commerce or easy management and lack the biodiversity of natural forests. They offer limited food, shelter and nesting sites. There is a better option. A meta-analysis found that plantations mixing several species would store more carbon, alongside other benefits.

nature-nbs-114.title: Succession: how restoration borrows nature's own recovery
nature-nbs-114.text: Bare ground rarely stays bare. Ecological succession is the way a community of living things changes over time, especially after a disturbance. Ecosystems often move from a few pioneer species, the first hardy arrivals, to a complex community of many interdependent species. Restoration often means starting, helping or speeding up that process, depending on how severe the disturbance was. After severe damage, such as in cities, restorers may first have to recreate the conditions that let succession happen at all.

nature-nbs-154.title: Secondary forest: the woods that grow back on their own
nature-nbs-154.text: Most forests of the United States and Europe are not ancient. They are secondary forest: woodland that has grown back largely by natural processes after logging, clearing for farming or a similar disturbance. It differs from old-growth, or primary, forest, which has not recently been disturbed. The comeback follows a sequence. Pioneer species take over cleared land first, then shrubs, and finally trees of the original forest. It typically takes 40 to 100 years to start to resemble the old-growth forest. Species numbers can recover quickly, but which species and how common they are take much longer. These forests do real work. They store more soil carbon than plantations, though less than primary forests. They protect watersheds, provide habitat, link forest fragments and supply wood to rural communities. By some estimates, more than 50 acres of new secondary forest grow for every acre of old-growth cut.

nature-nbs-121.title: Forest restoration: speeding a forest back toward maturity
nature-nbs-121.text: Active restoration can speed carbon recovery in human-modified tropical forests by as much as 50%. Forest restoration is action that speeds a forest's return toward a climax forest, the end stage of natural succession. Climax forests are fairly stable ecosystems with the most biomass, structure and species that climate and soil allow without human disturbance. Forest restoration is a special kind of reforestation. Its main goals are biodiversity recovery and environmental protection, unlike timber plantations. Methods range from protecting leftover vegetation, by preventing fire or keeping out cattle, to planting trees or sowing seeds directly. Success shows up as more biodiversity, biomass, productivity, soil organic matter and water-holding capacity, plus the return of rare and keystone species. It also has a money measure: the value of forest products and of services such as watershed protection and carbon storage. Payments for those services can give local people strong reasons to restore. Climate change complicates the target, because climate shapes climax forests.

nature-nbs-122.title: Forest landscape restoration: planning for people and wildlife
nature-nbs-122.text: One restored hillside helps little if the valley around it keeps degrading. Forest landscape restoration (FLR) is a planned process to regain ecological integrity and improve human well-being across deforested or degraded landscapes. It links work at single sites to goals for a whole landscape, agreed among stakeholders. The concept grew out of work by the IUCN, WWF, the World Resources Institute and the International Tropical Timber Organization. It seeks compromises between the needs of people and wildlife, with local communities central to planning. Desired outcomes include tackling root causes of degradation, settling land-use conflicts, agreeing how benefits are shared and providing watershed services. A program can mix protecting secondary forest, {{ref:nature-nbs-138}}, planting framework trees, timber plantations and growing trees with crops. In 2014 FAO set up a mechanism to help countries meet the {{ref:nature-nbs-139}}.

nature-nbs-139.title: The Bonn Challenge: a global pledge to restore land
nature-nbs-139.text: On 2 September 2011, Germany and the IUCN launched a global goal in Bonn. The Bonn Challenge aims to restore 150 million hectares of degraded and deforested land by 2020 and 350 million hectares by 2030. The promised returns are large. The IUCN estimates meeting it would bring about $84 billion a year in net benefits, helping rural incomes. It is estimated to shrink the carbon dioxide emissions gap by 11-17%. Reaching 350 million hectares could bring up to $9 trillion in net benefits. Pakistan's Billion Tree Tsunami restored 350,000 hectares, beating its pledge. Not every pledge is what it seems, though. Nearly half were found to be land set aside for commercial wood use.

nature-nbs-138.title: Assisted natural regeneration: helping forests regrow themselves
nature-nbs-138.text: Often the seedlings are already there, waiting for a chance. Assisted natural regeneration (ANR), or managed regrowth, is protecting and caring for tree seedlings that sprout naturally so a forest regrows. It removes barriers such as weeds, poor soil, fire-prone grasses like Imperata, and other disturbance. New trees go in only where needed, which is called enrichment planting. It is cheaper than replanting because it skips nurseries, site preparation and raising seedlings, and forests grow faster than alone. It needs enough natural seedlings (200 to 800 per hectare suggested), nearby seed sources and control of grazing, fire and logging. The weeding and firebreaks can create local jobs. A related method, farmer-managed natural regeneration, regrows trees from roots that survive in cleared land. Their seedlings survive better because the roots already reach groundwater.

nature-nbs-153.title: Passive rewilding: letting abandoned land go wild
nature-nbs-153.text: Wolves, lynxes, boars and brown bears have returned to the Chernobyl Exclusion Zone. No one put them there. Passive rewilding is letting land, usually after it has been abandoned, return to nature with little or no human management. It is also called natural or spontaneous regeneration, and unlike other rewilding, people do not intervene directly. It has three parts: letting wildlife return, reconnecting landscapes so plants and animals can move, and allowing disturbances such as fires, pests and floods. Land is left either on purpose or because of socio-economic change. Forests have been regrowing on abandoned pastures and scrub across Europe and North America. Results vary. In Spain, regrowth on abandoned farmland has raised fire risk, and effects on biodiversity depend on the site. In 1998 Bruce Sterling coined 'involuntary park' for once-inhabited places left to go wild.
